newsitem.title: USA: U.S. astronauts space walk to practise construction.
newsitem.headline: U.S. astronauts space walk to practise construction.

text.p: The space shuttle Columbia was set to become an orbiting construction site on Thursday night when two astronauts practise assembly of the planned international space station.

Astronauts Tammy Jernigan and Tom Jones were scheduled to venture into the shuttle's 60-foot (20 metres)-long cargo bay at about 9:20 p.m. EST (0220 GMT Friday) for the latest in a series of space walks to test tools and techniques needed for construction of the NASA-led, 13-nation space station.

"Of all the space station assembly missions coming up, probably more than 80 percent of them require (space walks)," Jones said. "They're going to depend on these concepts that we think we've gotten right, but we've got to prove."

Jernigan and Jones will operate an 18-foot (6-metre)-long crane to practise moving large space station batteries. The telescoping crane, controlled by three hand-turned cranks, will be used to lift and position a simulated battery.

Astronauts on a shuttle mission in March 1999 will use the crane to move four 586-pound (265 kg) batteries and two equally hefty charger-discharger devices about 80 feet (26 metres) from the shuttle's cargo bay to the end of the space station's long structure.
Although objects in space are described as being weightless, they still have mass. Once a heavy object starts moving it can be difficult to stop.

The telescopic crane, which is similar in design to two on the Russian space station Mir, will be used in conjunction with the more complex robot arms on the space station and shuttle to manage these bulky components.
The astronauts will also test a drill-like power tool, a foot restraint and other gear. The duo will make a second walk into space on Saturday night for more than six hours.

NASA estimates about 80 American space walks, totalling more than 630 hours, will be needed over the five-year construction effort, scheduled to get under way late next year. In addition, Russian cosmonauts will walk outside the international outpost about 30 times.
By comparison, U.S. astronauts have made 33 space walks, totalling about 400 hours, during the 15-year shuttle programme.

Veteran astronaut Story Musgrave, who will direct Thursday's spacewalk from inside the shuttle's cabin, believes the space agency is not ready for the increased space walking activity. More effort is needed to improve training facilities such as water tanks, vacuum chambers and virtual reality simulators, he said.
"We're going to have to ramp up those resources and capabilities to handle that amount of space walks," he said before the mission. "We're not there yet."
Musgrave, at 61 the oldest person ever in space, led the four-member space walking team that repaired NASA's Hubble Space Telescope in 1993 and also made the first shuttle space walk in 1983.

Columbia is being followed through space by a U.S.-German orbiting observatory, released from Columbia soon after its Nov. 19 blast off. The remotely operated Orfeus-Spas telescope was continuing to study the life cycles of the stars and the mysterious interstellar matter that lies between them.
The shuttle crew will intercept the telescope and stash it in the cargo bay two days before their planned Dec. 5 return to earth.
